utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We continue with the evidence. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence calls the next witness, Jovica Nesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you please take the card and read the affirmation that is on it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovica Nesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of September 1961 in Svilajnac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I'm a professional serviceman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When did you join the army service?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Since 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I would kindly ask you for the sake of interpreters and the transcript to wait a little before you give your answer to my question. Mr. Nesic, could you please tell us what education you have.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I finished elementary school, then high school. And after that, the military academy for ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any additional training or specialised training?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: So far, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, in 1991, where were you serving?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: In 1991 until almost late September, I served at the infantry school centre in Bileca. And then from the end of September 1991, I was stationed with the 472nd Motorised Brigade of the 9th VPS -- I apologise, it's not the motorised brigade, it was naval landing brigade, in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were stationed at the infantry reserve officers' school, what duties did you discharge there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: While I was serving in Bileca from 1986 until August approximately 1990, I was a platoon commander. And after that, from August 1990 until late September 1991, I was the instructor, firing instructor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you reside in Bileca as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In September 1991, were you transferred to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Initially, that was not a transfer. I was, rather, seconded to Trebinje. And after that, an order on transfer arrived for me to move to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since that was late September 1991, tell me, please, was any other of your colleagues, officers from Bileca, transferred to Trebinje, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, many of my colleagues were transferred. That is, practically the majority of them from Bileca to the Trebinje Brigade. I can give you some of the names of the people that I had most contacts while I was at the theatre. That was Captain Stojanovic, Sergeant Lemal, Sergeant Pesic, Captain Jeremic, Second-Lieutenant Hodza, Captain Denic. And many, many others. Among them was my neighbour, Zeljko Soldo who lived in a flat above me in the resident building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of these men, your colleagues from Bileca that you have just named, was with you in the same unit within the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the same battalion. I was there, so was Stojanovic, so was Lemal, so was Jeremic, Soldo, although he did join us later on sometime in November. But we were in the same unit, including Hodza, Sikimic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Trebinje to the 472nd Brigade, which was your position that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I was assigned commander of an anti-armour company of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the anti-armour company? Who was the commander of that company before you came?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Before I came, the commander of the anti-armour company was Reserve Captain Sutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the situation that you found upon your arrival at the company?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The situation was in a way good, but nonetheless it wasn't in keeping with my standards and my understanding of how a situation and a unit should be, that is, the standards that I acquired and applied while I worked in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this reflected, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was reflected in the inexperience of this reserve officer to establish full order in the units to deploy the firing pieces in proper way, to provide fortification of the unit in a proper manner, which I, after I had joined them, corrected and rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with the strength of the unit and the level of strength?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The unit was manned as per establishment fully; however, that was only in terms of numbers. One part of the unit was not properly trained for their duties because there were certain problems in that area, primarily for the reason of the 472nd Navy Landing Brigade was predominantly manned by reserve forces from Dubrovnik and Trebinje municipalities. And with the advent of this situation, this recruitment from the territory of Dubrovnik Municipality was not carried out so that all the planned military specialties that should have been there could not have been met. It was done only partially, whereas in the remaining problematic area, this was made up for by physical numbers of men. The strength of the unit consisted of 40 per cent active-duty officers and about 60 per cent of reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. An anti-armour company has what kind of weapons? What did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: My unit had six anti-armour, recoilless, 82-millimetre guns, and six anti-armour, 9K-11, self-guided missile launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that what is popularly known as Maljutka rockets?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct, although you cannot view it exactly in that way because if we say Maljutka that implies, and that refers to the rocket itself. Rocket is virtually only a charge, whereas the firing piece has a guiding device, and I had this kind of six guiding devices for this type of rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, who was the commander of that rocket platoon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the time when I arrived in the unit in late September, I believe it was the 25th or the 26th of September but I can't give you the exact date, the platoon commander, the rocket platoon commander, was Hodza Naser, Second Lieutenant Hodza Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, at which position was your company in late September and early October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At that time, my company was in the Ivanica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which republic was that in?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That is the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when combat operations commenced in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact date. It was early October. Whether it was the 1st or the 2nd, I can't really say. It was the 1st or the 2nd at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, how about your company? Did you suffer any casualties when combat operations first began?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the very first day of combat operations, there were ten people who were killed and two men were wounded in my company. Eight soldiers of the ten who were killed died on the spot while two succumbed to the wounds they had received, at the Trebinje hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it came about that those people were killed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. My unit's position came under fire by mortar projectiles, 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre projectiles. For the best part of the day, those projectiles kept overshooting the shelter behind which our soldiers were. But at one point, the mortar shell hit a gun crew directly, and five people were killed there. Just after that, the crew manning the adjacent gun realised what had happened to the first crew. They left their shelter and came out to pull out those people from their position. However, at that very moment, another 120-millimetre shell fell between them, so the other crew who came out to help was also hit, the gun crew. Alongside with them, the platoon commander at the time was also hit, a reserve lieutenant colonel -- a reserve second lieutenant and also the squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade right at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: When I came to the unit, the battalion commander was Captain First Class Ekrem Devlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The deputy was Captain Vladimir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In relation to that situation, did any changes occur in terms of the battalion command later on?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were changes. Sometime in the second half of October, I can't be more specific, the man who had been battalion commander up to that point, Captain Devlic, was wounded. And since he had to leave in order to receive proper treatments, Captain Kovacevic became battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, where was your company staying throughout October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of October up to just days before the end of the month, the company was at Ivanica. As for the last few days before the end of October, the 27th or 28th perhaps, but I can't be specific, the company was pulled out to the rear to rest. And this was at Talezi village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the Talez area, did at any point your battalion join in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early November, the first half of November, again, I can't give you the exact date, I'm sorry. It could have been the 7th or the 8th or possibly the 10th of November, so it was the first third of the month in a manner of speaking, we received the assignment to move out of the area where we were resting and to engage in combat in order to take the elevations surrounding the village and the village of Bosanka itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did your company do in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: From the moment we left the village of Talez until the moment we reached the village of Brgat, we kept on working as an anti-armour company. However, from the time we arrived in the village of Brgat, I received orders -- at the time we arrived in the village of Brgat, I received orders to leave our pieces behind and to keep on moving and to be at the ready to engage in further combat operations, but also to be ready to be used as a pure and simple infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did your company take Zarkovica at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in the Zarkovica area, because I had been going behind the remaining infantry units, I received orders to take shelter behind the tower at Zarkovica and to be at the ready and be prepared to join combat operations in the direction of the village of Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, by the time you reached Zarkovica at that time, did you find anyone there? Were there any soldiers or troops there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: By the time I reached Zarkovica, there were soldiers there who were members of other units, units that were not within the composition of our 3rd Battalion; more specifically, at Zarkovica, I found observers and the commander from the 130-millimetre gun battery that were stationed at Cilipi. I found a 120/3-millimetre anti-aircraft gun, a T-55 tank, some other soldiers, I didn't know which unit they were from. There was a motor vehicle there also that had been destroyed. It was a freight vehicle, T-70 -- 710.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you seized control of that feature at Zarkovica, was your unit fired upon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the moment when we reached Zarkovica, we were under heavy fire specifically. The tower at Zarkovica was targeted. And during that day, within the close perimeter and around the tower, 59 shells fell. No one really counted the shells in, those that fell around the tower. But as it happened, soldiers knew roughly how many shells fell just around the tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did those combat operations go on for in November?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The fighting in November lasted for two days. That's from the moment I arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which specific positions were taken up by your battalion once the fighting was over?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Once the fight was over, the line that we had reached was the Dubac/Zarkovica/Bosanka/Strincijera line, and also that other place in Rijeka Dubrovacka straddling the road, Cajkovici. Yes, that's the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the position at Zarkovica, were you able to observe the firing points of the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to observe their positions. First of all, Zarkovica itself was a dominant feature. And from there, you had a very clear view over at least half of Dubrovnik town, if not actually more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any reconnaissance or monitoring devices, equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to different optical devices, yes I did. I had a binocular that I had signed for. I had optical sighting equipment on each of the recoilless guns that we had. And we also used the artillery compass that was there that belonged to the unit, to the battery that I talked about. The commander was there before I came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I ask the witness be asked again. There was an omission in the record, and I'm not sure that we can pick it up later. It's page 10, line 5. "We also used the artillery" blank, and I'm not sure what the blank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you just repeat, or rather describe again what has been asked.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a periscopic artillery binocular.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, from Zarkovica, could you see the Old Town? Was it within the area that you could see from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything out of the ordinary in relation to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Out of the ordinary in the Old Town, well, it was empty. There were no people moving about, as was usual. Other than that, there was firing against our units from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We have no time frame for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll specify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, everything that we have been talking about is in relation to which period of time, between the 1st of October and 31st of December. But my specific question now, the last one, is from the time you arrived at Zarkovica as you said in November and on. So what you've just told us, is that in relation to the period of time between the time you came to Zarkovica in November?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding of your question, that you were referring to the specific day when I reached Zarkovica. That was my understanding. And that was the day that I was talking about, the day I arrived at Zarkovica. I have already given you the date, at least I was as specific as I could be. But I couldn't give you the exact date. It was around the 10th of November. I'm not sure if it was the 6th, the 7th, the 8th. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, what you've said about firing from the Old Town, that refers to those days when you came to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the very first day I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you provide more detail about what exactly you noticed in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, gladly. Specifically, I saw a machine-gun fire from the harbour. The exact location was just below the arch of the town's big cafe, facing one of streets in the Old Town. Secondly, there was firing also from the opposite side of the Old Town near one of the gates. The gate is called Pile. Four mortars from firing from there. Specifically, from where I was standing, I couldn't see the mortars themselves because they had -- they were sheltered. They were behind something. But we did see people moving about. And several days later, we received confirmation that mortars had indeed been active there in that very area because soldiers who led the front --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the last piece of evidence is not part of the 65 ter summary about any confirmation of anything later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Rodic, you might get clear what the witness could actually see in connection with this firing from the far side of the town near the Pile gate. And then we'll see where we go from there with this question of 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, now that you're talking about mortars that are positioned near the Pile gate, can you describe to us in greater detail what it was that you specifically noticed. What did you observe there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I observed the movement of uniformed persons in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This movement of uniformed persons, how do you relate this to the mortars that you could not see yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I relate the two for two reasons: The first reason is that in that area, we fired a projectile from a cannon into that area specifically. After the projectile fell there in that area, the mortar stopped firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And secondly --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The witness does not know there was a mortar. The witness saw movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position, Mr. Rodic, is not coming across in a satisfactory way. The witness is assuming something. What we need to know is what it is that he actually observed, if you could be more careful in the questioning to get that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I shall do that. The witness just tried to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, you described the movement of these persons and what you did and the action taken there. But since you yourself did not see what you mentioned just now, the four mortars, can you tell us how come you know that this involved four mortars rather than one or two, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I can explain. I've tried to explain a few times, but I was interrupted in making my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have to object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are reasons why you are being interrupted, Mr. Nesic, because we want to know only what you observed at this point and not what you deduced. If you can confine your evidence at the moment to what you yourself actually saw, thank you. Now, at the moment in my understanding of the evidence, Mr. Rodic, the witness has not seen any mortars or seen any firing of mortars. I'll leave you to proceed with your questioning from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, apart from this movement of persons that you described to us near the Pile gate, did you notice anything else specifically then?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Specifically at that place, I did not. However, infantry weapons were fired from the Old Town walls, and that could be heard clearly. Gunfire from infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I saw nothing in the 65 ter summary about infantry weapons being fired from the Old Town walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall proceed then. I shall --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. But Ms. Somers was not in Dubrovnik at the time, so she could not see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, please do not make any comments. Just do your best to answer my questions. Tell me, please, these persons that you observed near the Pile gate at that position, did you manage to see what kind of persons they were?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I could see. These were uniformed persons with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the usher's assistance. I would like the witness to be given this map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, could you please take the magic marker and mark the position of the machine-gun that you spoke of and the position relating to the movement of these uniformed persons that you also spoke of.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I'll try to mark that because this position, the picture of the Old Town, cannot be seen in the sense of the actual curve where it is. So I will mark the tactical sign that pertains to a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please mark that particular place with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, please mark where these people in uniform that you observed were moving.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Can this be marked by an arrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that particular position with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And finally, could you please put the date on this map and sign it.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The lower part or the upper part of the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Wherever there is enough room.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What's the date today?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this map please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map will be received, marked with two markings. One, the marking by the harbour of the machine-gun position the witness observed. And the other marking with an arrow where uniformed men were seen near the Pile gate. A third marking was placed near the arrow, but that is not the subject of direct evidence. I know what it signifies normally, and that is precisely the evidence to which objection is presently taken.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked D109.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, after the fighting was over in November, the fighting that you spoke of, you said that the fighting was over once your battalion had taken these positions. In the period after that, were there any fire provocations against your unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: There were fire provocations. Fire provocations occurred every day. It is infantry weapons that were fired. For the most part, these weapons had silencers, so you could not really hear the shot. Only bullets whizzing by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you carry out any observing from your positions in the course of the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. From these positions, we carried out observations every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what does the organisation of this observation within your company look like?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Specifically in my company, at the front end of the wall of the tower of Zarkovica, I had an observer on duty all the time. And they took turns every hour. This soldier, observer, was charged with the duty of observing the entire area in front of him, all the way to Dubrovnik, and to inform us of anything that he might notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When somebody else carried out these observations, when you did not, did you receive information about targets, objectives, anything that might have been observed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already mentioned there was an observer there all the time. And I would sometimes go out and carry out these observations myself. But the observer would report on what he had observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me specifically, please, about things like what you described to me, the firing of machine-gun coming from the Old Town. Did you report to anyone about that? Did you let anyone know about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: As for all more relevant information, more important information that we received, I would send it further on to the superior command; that is to say, to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to inform anybody else?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. My link goes to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in December 1991, did your battalion attack the positions of the Srdj fortress?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The battalion that I served in did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, can you tell us how this actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, sometime in the evening of the 5th, early evening - I cannot give you the exact time, what time it was exactly - I was in my unit at Zarkovica, and I was informed that I should go and report at the command, or rather that we would have a briefing held at the command of the commander of the mortar company, Captain Jeremic at Ivanica, to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who informed you of this and what were you told?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: A soldier, a communications soldier from the command informed me of this, the man who worked on these communications. And what was conveyed to me was what I already said, that I should go down to Ivanica for a briefing because the battalion commander is still at the Kupari briefing. And from Kupari, he would probably come there to Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you actually go to Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did your commander arrive there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the moment when I arrived, he was not at Ivanica yet. But soon after that, he did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what did the commander tell you during this briefing?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: After he arrived, he told us that we were given the task of taking Srdj the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he say who gave him this task?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The task was received at the forward command post in Kupari where he had attended a briefing. I don't remember him mentioning any specific names in terms of who charged him with this task. But when he came back from the command post, from this briefing, he told us that we were given the task of carrying out an attack on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did he tell you whether you would have any support, whether you would act in concert with someone when you carry out that task?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Of course. He gave us an order to that effect. This is an order that is issued to the company commanders. And he told us that due to constant provocations from that area, the basing of units there, then there was total control of the unit's movements, of our unit's movements from up there. So because of all of that, we were supposed to take this feature of Srdj. Also, he said that in addition to our own forces, we would be supported with a 130-millimetre battery, that is to say, a battery of 130-millimetre cannons from the area of Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you presented the plan of this action, of this attack, were you all given specific tasks within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. The plan was presented, or rather, it was an order in military terminology. It contained specific tasks of each unit, very precise tasks for each company and what it was supposed to do as part of the overall mission. And I can repeat which individual unit was given a task, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The company of Captain Stojanovic and Sergeant -- were given the task to form combat groups for the attack on Srdj. Under such circumstances, it was tactically fully justified because it could not have been done with a large-size unit because the people would be congested. That is why smaller units were used. Both units, the one commanded by Captain Stojanovic and the other commanded by Sergeant Lemal, were supposed to be supported by one tank each. They were instructed to advance behind the tank in order to hide from the fire coming from Srdj. The tank was supposed to neutralise firing points that may be on the wall, and they were to proceed in that manner until they reached the fortress itself. So these two groups advanced from two directions. One was led by Captain Stojanovic, and it was moving from the direction of Bosanka towards Srdj. And the one led by Sergeant Lemal, from Strincijera, Bosanka, and then to Srdj. Then a mortar company was given a task to carry out firing preparation for the attack which means that they were told to target the fortress on Srdj itself and not to allow the men to leave the Srdj fortress because we estimated there were quite a few men there. And to fire in front of the fortress itself with a view to possibly opening a passage through the mined field that had been planted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you here, tell me, do you know who was supposed to lead the group from Bosanka towards Srdj?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Sergeant Pesic -- sorry, Lieutenant Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In this order, what was the task of your anti-armour company -- just a moment, please. There is no answer that you gave to my question who was commanding the company at Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The company commander at Bosanka was Captain Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Within the terms of this task, what was the anti-armour company supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The anti-armour company had the duty to secure the left flank on the southern slopes of Srdj towards the town. So virtually to control this area and to prevent the units moving forward to Srdj to come under fire. Their duty was also to prevent bringing fresh forces from Dubrovnik to Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any special requests for any special equipment required for this mission?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I myself didn't have any specific requests, but the company commanders did have requests. They requested to be issued bulletproof vests, tear gas, bombs, explosives and things like that that we were not issued as per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they had received all these required equipment for this specific mission?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. Captain Stojanovic received bulletproof vests. They were, in fact, left with me in Zarkovica, and then he came from Bosanka to Zarkovica and took them and took them to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know who had left these bulletproof vests with you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly because they were taken over by my sergeant who was keeping the duty, and he said that a vehicle had come from Kupari, that he had received this consignment, and that he had left it in my so-called office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when the attack on Srdj began.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The attack began on the following day in the early morning hours. I cannot say exactly at what hour. But it was at dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the time, who was in Zarkovica at the positions of the anti-armour company?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to other units?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Besides my unit was the commander of the battalion in Zarkovica. He set up his observation post. There was also the company commander of the 130-millimetre gun battery from Cilipi. And there was also one of the officers - I cannot remember his name - from the forward command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when the operation conducted by the 3rd Battalion commenced against Srdj, were there any counterfire coming from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which positions were targeted by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the attack itself began, a few mortar shells were fired towards Zarkovica. One of the shells -- none of the shells hit the fortress, but rather landed near it. Immediately thereafter, they engaged all the weapons that they had and targeted Srdj with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: From the Zarkovica position, what directions were you able to observe on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It's a very broad term, but if I take that my right limit of vision was the road to Srdj and the fortress itself, and on the left-hand side it was the sea, therefore I could view the whole area of the town from where I was standing and beyond the whole area that I could observe as far as the Petka cape.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What kind of communications equipment did you have at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: My company had radio sets, RUP-12, that we used to communicate with the battalion command. We had also a RUP-3 to serve as a communication device between me and platoon commanders. And I also had a field telephone which I used to communicate with the command at Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, was this communication working?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, between me and the battalion commander and between me and other platoon commanders. However, during the day, we did not use it extensively, but we rather reduced our communication to using couriers or direct contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have -- this wire telephone, induction telephone that you had on Zarkovica, was it operational?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: During the night, it did. However, from the very early morning at about 0400 hours or 0430 when I left this area onward, I cannot say for sure because I stopped using it altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anyone inform you whether there were any problems with this wire telephone?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on that day, did you notice firing targets of the Croatian forces following the commencement of the operation against Srdj?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: On that day, I noticed several targets. I noticed them as well as other soldiers who observed them and who reported on that. Specifically, I personally noticed a mortar at the fortress, that is, the farthest fortress in the south, which became immediately active in the morning. Then later in the day, I also noticed that crates had been carried out with some sort of ammunition from the area of fish market at the entrance to the Old Town --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's no evidence that there was ammunition in any crates that may or may not have been seen. If the witness is saying that he saw crates, that may be one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Rodic, we have this trouble between assumption and what was actually observed. You'll have to be much more careful with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, both in the summary, it was mentioned what kind of crates were there. But he did not specifically say what the contents on the crates were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, the witness at the moment saw crates. That is the evidence. He is adding something about their content. Now, either from the physical description of the crate, he might base a conclusion, or he is otherwise simply assuming. So understand at the moment, the admissible evidence is that he saw crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, when you were describing seeing crates being carried out, could you tell us, please, what kind of crates those were? Was there any characteristic feature on those crates? Did you notice anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The characteristic feature of these crates is that they were of the characteristic olive-drab colour used by military, and secondly they were large-sized crates so that two men had to carry one crate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that the crates were rather large, painted in olive-drab colour used by military, can you tell us what this SMB abbreviation means?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That means olive-drab colour that mostly all military items are painted in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the JNA, tell me, what is the purpose of this type of crate?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: These crates are normally used for packing large-calibre ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, you saw men carrying in and out these crates. Did you see what was inside the crates?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you described the position. Can you tell us more specifically where you were while you observed these crates being carried in and out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: They were carried out from the so-called fish market at the entrance to the Old Town from the side of the port, and they were carried to the entrance to the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Sometime around noon, fire was opened at us from an anti-aircraft gun from the area to -- of the right-hand tower in the Old Town port.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you, when you mentioned the mortar at the south tower facing the sea, was this mortar opening fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you see where it was firing at?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could, since vis-a-vis my position, it was positioned laterally, and it was firing at Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the anti-aircraft gun that you said you noticed firing? Could you tell what it was firing at?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The anti-aircraft gun was firing in the general direction of my unit, but a little to the left, seawards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please show the witness a map that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you please first of all mark on the map the position at which you noticed the mortar.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that spot with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next, can you please use arrows to indicate the exact position where the crates that you referred to were carried to and from.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I don't think this map is very accurate. Right here, there is a breakwater in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would that make it impossible for you to mark it on the map?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, no, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to that arrow, can you please put the number 2 to mark the position where these crates were being moved in and out.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were they being moved into the Old Town, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Through that passage there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Finally, can you please mark the position of the anti-aircraft gun when you noticed it firing.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: On this wall right here, there are three openings of windows. You can't see them on the map. Therefore, there was firing from the tower itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to that mark, is that the mark you made for the anti-aircraft cannon?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you put the number 3 there also, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you put today's date on this map, the 19th of July, and please sign.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this map please be received as a Defence exhibit before we head for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, before the break, you marked for us on the map the firing positions that you noticed inside the Old Town on the day when the attack on Srdj took place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, from your position at Zarkovica, in addition to the Old Town, did you notice any other firing points outside the Old Town nucleus?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which ones.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: From the area around the Lovrinac tower, there is a tunnel there and a small park. I saw artillery pieces firing from there. Further, in about the same area, I was at an angle but it was somewhere behind the Libertas Hotel, there was a clearing there from which four mortars were firing. Also, there was firing from the lower road. This is a road running parallel to the main road just above Dubrovnik. There was a Flying Charlie-type of mortar moving about. Flying Charlie is a name we used for that particular mortar; it was mounted on a vehicle, a small truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection, Your Honour. A Flying Charlie reference is not in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, it is stated accurately in the summary that this witness would testify about such firing positions as were observed and the activities of the Croatian forces from inside the Old Town, and then the weapons and pieces were enumerated that he had observed. And in the summary, it is clearly stated that the witness would testify about the firing positions and the activities of the Croatian forces outside the Old Town, that is, the Old Town nucleus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is this you're referring to, Mr. Rodic? In the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the summary that we sent to our colleagues from the OTP in relation to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is certainly nothing in the summary that the Chamber has received from you from the 65 ter. There's something beyond that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. This is a summary of the proofing session with this witness before -- prior to his appearance in court, and this has been submitted to our friends and colleagues from the OTP. If the Trial Chamber so wishes, I can give you this copy to look at which states precisely what I said in relation to this witness's testimony concerning the firing positions and the firing by Croatian units outside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you accept that all that was said in this further summary is that he would testify about the activities and the firing positions of Croatian forces outside the Old Town without any specification?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is quite correct that not all the firing targets outside the Old Town are specified for the simple reason that there were quite a number of such targets. And my learned friend only reacted once this mobile piece was mentioned or referred to, which is also a fire target outside the Old Town. When the witness spoke about mortars that were firing from outside the Old Town as well, there was no reaction on their part simply because both falls under the category of Croatian forces firing from outside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may read to the Chamber what was indicated: "He will further testify as to the cited fire positions and activities of the Croatian forces on the 6th of December 1991 that had been taken place outside the Old Town." The Charlie is a very specific aspect of testimony, and I think it's perfectly expected that if that is going to be included, that that be specified. Hardly a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have difficulty with that distinction, Ms. Somers. I think the evidence should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, you have so far mentioned the Lovrinac tower area. So right of that, the Libertas Hotel, a clearing with mortars, and then you said the lower road running parallel to the main road above. And here, you referred to the Flying Charlie. Were there any other targets that you observed that were outside the Old Town nucleus on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: There were other targets, one of them being a mortar firing from the park behind the Imperial Hotel. Also, there was a minefield straddling the main Adriatic road just below the forest on Srdj. And there was another mortar in the Excelsior Hotel area facing the Old Town which I suppose is west.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have to express an objection, Your Honour. None of these positions were put to the Witness Negodic, and if they were in fact known they were not put to that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sure you will remember cross-examination of Witness Negodic. We raised issues precisely in connection with the Bogosica Park or the Gradac Park with the Flying Charlie, which was the name used for a mortar that was mounted on a truck, also issues in relation to an anti-aircraft gun that was also mounted on a vehicle. There was also another issue raised in relation to positions near the Excelsior Hotel and that was marked on the map that was used during his testimony and received in evidence. And he spoke about the 6th of December specifically and the firing by that particular weapon at that particular position. So I'm sure Witness Negodic was examined on these points by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My recollection partly accords with yours, Mr. Rodic. But as I recall it, a number of positions now being identified were not specifically put to him. And it goes without saying he is the most obvious witness to whom such matters ought properly to have been put.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you're saying you had a full briefing from the present witness, and as I understand your submission, you are saying that you put to the Witness Negodic the effect as you knew it of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Rather, during the cross-examination of Witness Negodic, we asked questions about the Croatian forces' targets in the Dubrovnik town area that we knew of and that we were aware of. As for the witness currently in front of you, may I remind you that this witness was originally on the OTP witness list. And at one point in time, the Prosecution gave up the idea of calling this witness. It was only once the Prosecution case was over that the Defence had an opportunity to contact this witness and talk to him in relation to his potential testimony in this case and his knowledge of events from that period of time, specifically in the Dubrovnik and Herzegovina theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would submit, Your Honours, that even in the information that was gathered by the Prosecution from this witness, a number of these positions were not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, Ms. Somers, is not a proper submission to put.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The fact that the witness Negodic was the correct person to be there and that all possible targets could have been explored has not yet, in my view, been explained by my learned counsel, my friend opposite. There has been so much -- there were a number of hotels that were in the area. There were a number of positions. And we do not see that it should for the first time be raised now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I think the evidence should proceed, especially and principally because this was a Prosecution witness, and I accept from what Mr. Rodic has said, the Defence for the first time spoke to him after the close of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I wish to show the witness a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a map already in evidence or a new map, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a new map. And it has not been admitted into evidence so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I would prefer to use the one that has already been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you please use this map to mark the Zarkovica position which is where you were.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to that position, can you put the letter A.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you please mark the location in the Lovrinac tower area. You referred to a tunnel and to a small park.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you marked there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It's a tactical sign denoting an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the letter B there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be zoomed in at all? Sorry to interrupt, but it's very difficult to see anything from here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To the right of that position, at the back, the Libertas Hotel and a clearing where you said you saw a number of mortars, four mortars specifically. That's what you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that location.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to that sign, can you please put the letter C.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The following position that you referred to, you said it was the lower road running parallel to the main road where you saw the Flying Charlie moving about.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you used an arrow, and you drew an arrow towards that sign there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, halfway down the arrow I marked the mortar that was driving back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to that sign, can you please put the letter D.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a park behind the Imperial Hotel. Can you please mark that, too.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please place the letter E next to that mark.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The next was the minefield on the Adriatic road below the forest on Srdj. Can you mark that locality, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please place the letter F there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a mortar near the Excelsior Hotel towards the left in the direction of the Old Town. Could you please mark that position.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please put the letter G there.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, since you used the Cyrillic alphabet when you wrote all of this, could you please put the letter 1 next to the letter A, and then could you go on putting number 2 next to the letter B, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Next to C, number 3. Next to the letter D, number 4. Next to F, number 5. And next to the letter G, number 6.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You put number 7 somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: By the letter E. The area behind the Imperial Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be number 5, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, did you mark Zarkovica with a particular number?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So then numbers start from Zarkovica, if it's that way, then it's all right. All the letters have received appropriate numbers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this map, and could it please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D111.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, on the 6th of December, to the best of your knowledge, was the artillery firing, or rather 130-millimetre cannons?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: 130-millimetre cannons were not firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were orders being issued to have those cannons fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us, how come?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The battery commander of the 130-millimetre gun battery from Cilipi, on that day, as I've already mentioned, was at Zarkovica. He and I were close to each other during combat. We were at a distance of about 20 metres. As the mortars fired from the area behind the Libertas Hotel, certain observations were made. I personally came to Captain Pepic [phoen], the commander of the battery, and I showed him the target from where the fire was coming. I used an artillery compass, a periscope artillery compass, and I guided it to the target. He read the elements from the compass, and spoke to his assistant at the observation post. He gave him the appropriate elements that he then conveyed to the firing position in order to have all the firing elements there. After that, a report came from the firing position that the elements were taken, and he ordered the guns to be charged and fired. We observed the area where the shells were supposed to fall, but there weren't any. He then insisted. He called the firing position again, and he asked what was going on, why they were running late. First, they told him that they were waiting. And then, when he asked again what was going on and why fire was not being opened and what the problem was, he was given an answer, and I can't remember the name of the officer who gave this answer, but anyway somebody, an officer, came from the forward command post. He came in person, and he did not allow fire to be opened from these cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you -- when you mentioned a firing position from where 130-millimetre guns were supposed to fire, what location are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: This is the location of the airport of Cilipi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Captain Kovacevic give you any orders with regard to opening fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: On a few occasions, Captain Kovacevic ordered me to find these pieces that were firing at our units and to neutralise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you receive such orders only once during the day or --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Several times during the day. The more intensive fire came to the area of Srdj, this was insisted upon more and more. "Find them, see where they're firing from. Cover that position with our own fire," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: On that day, was Captain Kovacevic moving about in the plateau of Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: He was not moving about, at least not in the area where I was, because he was in this office of mine, if we are going to call it that. This is actually one of the towers at Zarkovica from where he was observing and commanding combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on that day, did Captain Kovacevic personally fire rockets from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That day on Zarkovica, while this attack against Srdj was underway, did you see any other officers there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: First of all, I saw, of course, the commanders from my own unit. Then in addition to Kovacevic, Battleship Captain Zec was there, too, and another officer, a naval officer; I really cannot remember his name. From the battalion command, there was Captain Soldo. And then this officer who I already mentioned, Captain Pepic from the 130-millimetre battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, during the morning, say, until midday, did anybody order you to stop firing?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know how and when the Srdj action was completed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The action at Srdj was completed after no support came from the 130-millimetre guns. There was no possibility for these mortars to be neutralised. They were incessantly firing at the Srdj plateau, so units were sustaining losses. After that, orders were issued for the units to withdraw from Srdj to their own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of losses the 3rd Battalion had sustained?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: There were seven dead and five wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed from your company?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about that? Are you sure about what you said, what you said just now, the figures you gave for the dead and wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I think I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were there any reactions among the troops when this action was completed, or rather when the withdrawal from Srdj took place?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few expressions of dissatisfaction because the task was not completed successfully. People got killed, and the task was not carried out. So for the most part, everybody was dissatisfied, especially because we did not get support from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Your Honour, the witness said "promised support," but that is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, did any higher ranking officers outside the 3rd Battalion, those who were not in the 3rd Battalion, did they come to see the units of that battalion on that day or later on?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: In the evening, that is to say, when it got dark, some officers from the superior command did come, and they were focussed in Lemal's and Stojanovic's units because that is where there were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did such activities take place in the days after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. There were several visits, contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, could you please look at this document and could you please tell us what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Could we clarify whether this is a resubmitted or a recalled document, or is this a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a Defence document from the 65 ter list of documents that was submitted to the Prosecution. Until now, it has not been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, the Prosecution would like to register its objection. This is a 9th VPS document that was not presented to Admiral Jokic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you tell me what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: This is a combat document which is drafted every day by the command in order to report to the superior command. Specifically here, it is the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector from the forward command post of Kupari reports to the command of the 2nd Operational Group about what happened during the day of the 7th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 4. "Morale" is the heading. Is there any report of a visit to your battalion there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Officers from the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector visited the soldiers of the 3rd Battalion, the 472nd Naval Brigade and spoke to them. "The losses which this unit has sustained have unfavourably influenced its state of morale. The state of the situation in the unit and its trust in the unit command have not deteriorated. The unit feels fatigue due to the prolonged stay under very onerous circumstances".

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You say that high-ranking officers from the 9th VPS visited you. Were they trying to alleviate the feeling of loss in your unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: In the battalion, yes. They were talking to officers, soldiers, and I already said that they focussed on the company of Captain Stojanovic and the company of Lieutenant Lemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D112.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, after the 6th of December, were you with your unit, your company, and your battalion on subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Concerning the action on Srdj, the attack on Srdj that took place on the 6th of December, did anyone ask you to make any kind of statement, submit a report, or researched anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of December, I was informed by the battalion commander, Captain Kovacevic, that I should come to the command post at Brgat where, together with him, I would go for the debriefing at the Kupari forward command post where we would be requested to give an explanation for the firing at targets carried out on the previous day, or rather on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who else was supposed to go to the Kupari forward command post with the commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Myself, Captain Jeremic, and he himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Kupari? And if you did, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: We went to Kupari. At first, we entered the operations room where the debriefing session was to take place. All the officers were gathered there that normally attend these kind of sessions. Those were the officers from the forward command post at Kupari and commanders of subordinate units as well. When the session began, the Warship Captain Zec asked us to explain what had happened with Dubrovnik, which targets had been engaged. And after about 1 minute or so of discussion where each target was, I was ordered to leave the room and to make a written report on the events that I had started to explain at the meeting, including the expenditure of ammunition and the targets engaged on that day. I left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before that, tell me, please, who was chairing this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Warship Captain Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was his position at the 9th VPS command?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: He was chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When Captain Zec told you, ordered you to write this report, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I left the operations room and sat in the corridor and wrote the report. Then one of the officers - I don't remember his name - exited from the operations room, took my report, took it back to the operations room, and I left outside waiting until the meeting was over. And after that, I returned to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did Captain Jeremic write a report?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While the two of you were writing your respective reports, where was Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Captain Kovacevic was in the operations room together with other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he had written any report?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After that, did you return to your unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. We returned each to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After 6th of December, was Captain Kovacevic with the battalion on the subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the reply the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear my last question? On the subsequent days, was Captain Kovacevic with the unit of the 3rd Battalion after 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard your question. And I answered yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We didn't -- it wasn't recorded in the transcript. That is why I repeated the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you tell us, please, what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: This is the report that I wrote at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this is the report that you had just mentioned preparing on the 8th of December 1991 at the Kupari forward command post. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this report contain information about the targets and the expenditure of ammunition by your unit on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Both about the information about the ammunition and the targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask that this document be given a number as a Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked as D113.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, did you have regular reportings in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were these sessions held?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It depends. Sometimes these debriefing sessions were held at the battalion command, or sometimes the battalion commander would visit each unit and receive reports directly from them in which way he didn't have to gather all the commanders at one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did your commander go someplace for debriefing?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion went for debriefing to the forward command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the 13th or the 14th of December, was your battalion visited by General Strugar, Panic, and Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At any time in December 1991, did the three generals or two generals and the admiral come to visit your positions?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were at your position with your battalion, was it ever visited by General Strugar, Panic, and Admiral Jokic together?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, together. That took place in late March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
