utterances.text: Can you tell us where they came to visit you.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: They came to see me at Zarkovica. We sat in my office at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who else was present there from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Captain Stojanovic was there. Lieutenant Pesic and Captain Soldo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did any of the generals on that occasion propose or suggest that any of company commanders of the 3rd Battalion should be decorated or commended?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that something like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After the 6th of December and with respect to these events, were you ever decorated or promoted?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that visit of the three generals, what was the topic of your discussion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: We discussed the situation in general, and then we, the officers, complained about our unsolved status in the unit because despite a long period of time that we had already been at the position, that is about six months, we were still being registered at being stationed at our home unit in Bileca and that we were temporarily transferred there. We complained about this ambiguous status which precluded us from exercising our rights that we would normally be entitled to in the normal transfer, and that is what we complained about and pointed out that if anything should happen to any of us, officially in the documents we were not there where we were actually were, but rather we were in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you present this problem to General Panic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We reported this problem to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this request of yours or this problem solved?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was solved immediately the following day. First, it took six months. And then after this discussion, everything was solved in one day. We received all the necessary documents, duly signed on our transfer, and all the rights entailing from that. So everything was settled and resolved within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nesic, tell me, please, you are an experienced serviceman. In daylight, is it possible to see fire at the muzzle of a mortar while firing? Could that be seen with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's very visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the calibre of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, it does depend somewhat in terms that it affects the size of the flash. But regardless of the calibre, it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my colleague Petrovic to play for a few seconds from P66 evidence. And that's footage tendered through the witness Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the technical service please tell us how we can see this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can hear the sound, but there is no picture on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Someone is apparently on their way to deal with the technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. While we are waiting for that, I would ask another question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can a mortar fire from a solid surface?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What kind of solid surfaces can serve for using mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It can fire from an ice ground, from concrete or asphalt surface. It first has to be prepared beforehand to fire from this kind of surface. And if you have enough time to follow the whole procedure of placing sand or earth, it can normally operate as from any other surface of normal hardness. If you don't have enough time, it can be prepared by placing it on the surface which has been reinforced with sandbags or earthbags. But if you don't even have time for that, as a last resort, one of the crew will stand on the surface, hold the barrel, and the assistants and the sightman will operate the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can the surface be fixed in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I said yes. If you make it more heavy depending on the type of the terrain, you can use a wall or any other feature that you lean the bipod on it because that is where all the pressure is when the shell is fired, whereas other parts of the mortar does not sustain this kind of shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, you worked as an instructor at the Bileca school for reserve officers. These things that you've just told us about, these different possibilities, are they described anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the rules pertaining to 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you teach your cadets about these possibilities of using 82-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we taught them about that, those who were trained in the summer period were trained for using mortars on stone-ground because the area around Bileca is mostly stone. And also in the winter period, we trained them to use mortars on frozen ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to finish off by showing this short recording. And that would then conclude our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid wasting valuable time, if I may make a proposal: We would like to show this short recording in our redirect, if that is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Rodic, that the problem be dealt with over the next break and that at a convenient time to the Prosecution, you might interrupt the Prosecution's cross-examination to play it so that the Prosecution can then deal with this in the course of their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that conclude your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, indeed it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I note, Mr. Rodic, it took almost double the estimated time. You're going to have to do better than that during this week if we are to finish. Ms. Somers, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Nesic.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I hope you're feeling better. We know you were not well last week, and we hope you've recovered. Colonel, exactly --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- exactly when was Zarkovica taken by the forces of the 2nd Operational Group? Exactly when?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The exact day when Zarkovica was taken, I can't give you the exact date because I did not take part in the operations that led to the taking of Zarkovica. I reached Zarkovica with my unit when it had already been taken. Therefore, I merely came there and deployed my unit there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you at least assist us in telling us whether it was in October or November or what operations that were undertaken by the forces of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That was in early November, sometime around the 5th, 6th, 7th, perhaps the 8th of November. But it was around that time. As for the specific operations undertaken by the 2nd Operational Group in that period of time, I really can't say anything about that because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of what units did take Zarkovica? Do you know how it came to be taken?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I told you I don't know. I can't remember something I don't know. That was before I reached Zarkovica. If you mean whether those were units from our battalion, the answer is no, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, how -- you were -- if I understand your evidence correctly, you were based on Zarkovica. That was your post. You were there. Were you given to understand how long it had been in the hands of the forces of the 2nd Operational Group before you arrived there? I mean, had the area been recently taken? What was your understanding, if my question could be refined a bit more, of the situation around Zarkovica? Was it a freshly taken area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The situation at Zarkovica before I reached Zarkovica is something that I knew as good as nothing about. I told you that I had set out with my units to be used as an infantry unit in the operations around the village of Bosanka. As soon as I reached Zarkovica, my unit was held there. I told my men to take shelter, and I was at the ready for the continuing attack and for engaging towards the village of Bosanka and on towards Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I put to you that Zarkovica was already in the hands of the forces of the 2nd Operational Group by the end of October, would that help jog your memory about the conditions or the situation around Zarkovica at that time when you got there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't jog my memory. I told you about the situation I found at that position at the time when I reached the position with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a look, please, at two Prosecution exhibits and one Defence exhibit. P119, P121, and D112, please. Colonel, if you have in front of you those three documents, do you have them, all three? Do you have all three of them? Okay, I'll wait just a second.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I have all three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much. Can you take a look at the one that has Exhibit P119, which is dated the 24th of October 1991. It is an order that was issued by General Strugar. It is in evidence, so I'm not going to ask you about whether it should go into evidence. It's in evidence. And it is addressed to the 2nd Corps, the 37th Corps, the 9th VPS, and it says 472nd Mtbr. Do you see that? Under command, it says -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you take the Exhibit P121, which is a document also issued by General Strugar, also in evidence, which is from the 23rd of October. And it also -- it is addressed to the 9th VPS and it says the 472nd Mtbr. Do you see that as well, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the document that Defence counsel put to you today which is D112, it is a report from the 7th of December 1991. And it's -- it purports to have Captain Zec's signoff on it. Do you have that one in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, hang on. I may have to back off on that one. I may have given you the wrong number. Let's look at the other two. Let's look at the other two first. I'm sorry I may have confused you on that. Now, on the first that I showed you from General Strugar, the reference to 472nd Mtbr, now is that the unit, the brigade, to which your company belonged? Are we talking about the same brigade? I'm sorry, Colonel, is that the same brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the brigade within whose composition there was the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What does the abbreviation "Mtbr," what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It stands for navy brigade, infantry. Or rather...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you actually give us for each letter what the abbreviation means, what the M means, the T, the B, the R.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I apologise. MTBR, motorised brigade. The abbreviation stands for motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's right. Now, is there a particular reason that you referred when you first came during direct examination to a naval landing brigade? Why are you using that terminology when you see that it is not the going term?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That was an expression that I used because the brigade at Trebinje had always been a navy landing brigade. And naval infantry units were always trained in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But that's not the name of the brigade to which you belonged, is it? Or was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the time, the name of the unit was changed to motorised. I really don't know. But I know from an earlier period, because Trebinje was only 24 kilometres away from those two places, we were in contact with those officers from Trebinje. And I know that they had always been a navy landing brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I actually --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask to see D44, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to ask you in just a second a question about this. Can you look, please, at a document which is in evidence which comes from Jevrem Cokic. Do you know who Jevrem Cokic was, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the time, he was commander of the 2nd Operational Group. I'd know this general back from a time when he was still colonel, and he taught me back at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So this document is dated the 29th of September, which is - oh, gosh - a month or so before the other documents. And if you take a look on page - and I have the English only - but it's paragraph 2, item (b). Do you see that, paragraph 2, item (b) where it says "the 472rd Mtbr"? Now, even at that point in time it is referred to as -- right, as the Mtbr. Now, when you -- are you suggesting that you did not know the name of the formation to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The exact name, the 472nd or something-like-that brigade, I know it was the 472nd brigade. In our lingo, that's how we called it. It's only in official documents, then you state the full name. But colloquially, when referring to brigade, company, and battalion names, we used these. Therefore, it was customary for us to refer to it as a navy landing brigade. And that's why I called it that. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Old Town was shelled between 10 and 13 November 1991, the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Did you participate in the shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, Madam, not during the shelling. I did not take part in the shelling. Not at the time you have just given.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was your unit between the 10th and the 13th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The unit was at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it was the only unit on Zarkovica at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: As a unit, yes. The only unit. And as I said before, there were some other elements at Zarkovica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were the only unit that had the ability to fire Maljutkas between 10 and 13 November 1991 from Zarkovica, were you not, your unit that you commanded?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you -- strike that. The cost of a Maljutka, can you give us approximately the cost of both the launchers and the ammunition or the rockets that are used.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't give you a specific answer as to the cost. In our lingo, whenever we talked, we used to say that it cost approximately the same as a Jugo vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is an expensive bit of ammunition, isn't it? It's an expensive rocket? It's not your average, run-of-the-mill projectile?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite like that. The price is a lot lower than we said. But we just tried to get the crews and the operators to do their best during training so that they could properly guide rockets in combat. The real price would have been lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, in training, were the units that were being trained ever permitted to fire a live Maljutka in training?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify, which particular unit do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Units which were being trained to use the Maljutka as a weapon, was there live projectile training, or was it all through simulator?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Primarily, it's not a unit that fires as a unit. It's the operator who fires. And also, there is the preparatory period during which an operator is trained. For an operator to fire a missile, that is to say, a war missile, he has to train doing it 10.000 times on a simulator. And it is only then that he can actually fire a warhead or a missile.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many operators in a class of persons trained on Maljutkas are actually allowed to fire live projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Depends on the unit where the training took place. Some were more; some were less. But usually from one unit, from one platoon, there would be one operator who would be doing the firing, the one who was the best during training.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But that would not necessarily be the operator who ultimately in real combat does the firing; one of the other persons who maybe doesn't have live ammunition fires, isn't that correct? Persons who were not trained with live munitions can actually fire, and do, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Of course. Because every one of them is trained for such action. During the training itself, a selection of personnel takes place. For example, 30 people train as operators. But out of these 30 trainees, 7 or 10 or 5 men actually get the title of operator, whereas the rest get a VES, which is assistant operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But of those 5 who actually get the title of operator, perhaps only one has ever in the course of his training fired a live Maljutka projectile. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That's right. Perhaps not even one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, there has been evidence put before this Chamber that the Old Town was shelled or was hit by Maljutkas in November of 1991, between 10 and 13. You have indicated that your unit was the only unit up with Maljutkas in position. Did you ever report to any of your persons in the chain of command that you had fired upon the Old Town of Dubrovnik in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, when we discussed this in Belgrade, I told you and I'm telling you now again that my people did not shell Dubrovnik. We targeted firing objectives only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I put to you, Colonel Nesic, that you, of course, did shell Dubrovnik. And I ask you again: Was any action -- was any report made to any superiors about the activities of your unit with regard to the Old Town of Dubrovnik between 10 and 13 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Every day during briefings, I reported to my battalion commander about what had taken place during the course of the day, which targets were fired at during the day, what was observed, et cetera. So of course, the quantity of ammunition used and against which objectives is something that was brought up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was the list of targets at which your weapons were aiming also brought up to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: If you mean in writing, then no. Orally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever held accountable for the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik between 10 and 13 November 1991? By "accountable," I mean investigated, charged criminally, court-martialed, or any other form of discipline for serious violations of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I inquire as to when the Chamber plans to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A moment we set a convenient time, and that is now, I think. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed by counsel opposite that they have been able to get the material ready. So they have asked that now perhaps they can show the portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic, would you resume your examination-in-chief to deal with that video, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I shall be brief. Everything is fine technically speaking now. And could everybody please switch on to "computer evidence" on their monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nesic, could you please look at the footage that will be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you see the footage? Can you see it on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you recognise the piece there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. 82-millimetre mortar. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In this footage, you saw the firing of this mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When the mortar was fired, could a flare be seen at the barrel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I saw it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since this was taken close up, can this flare be seen better if you're even further away from the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: If you are further away and in the direction from where --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection. Objection. It is leading, highly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesic, can you tell us about the flare that appears at the barrel of the mortar when it fires in relation to the mortar itself. From where can this flare be seen the best?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: At the -- the flare from the muzzle can be seen the best if you are in a position from where you can view the muzzle directly. You can see it the best when it is nighttime, and also then further on if there is less light. The closer you are to the mortar, you can see only this momentary flare. But when there is less light generally speaking, then the flare from the mortar goes about 1 and a half metres from the muzzle of the mortar barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nesic, now we are going to play the same footage for you, but from a distance. Now, please, look at these particular videoclips and see whether you're going to see any flares or any such thing. Please pay attention to this when the Minceta fortress is shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can play it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a brief videoclip.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to see it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I saw your picture on the screen. So now again, I see the mortar picture in Bogosica Park. It is pretty vague anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll try again. We'll try to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Pay attention to the following footage now. Can you tell us whether you saw something?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I saw over here from the shadow, from among the trees a flare could be seen. It was about this big on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded in relation to this particular videoclip. Thank you. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. May I just perhaps point out this is P66, the 20th minute and 40th second. So the last was a clip where Minceta could be seen and where the witness recognised the firing of a mortar and he indicated the flare that appeared in the footage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that was at 20 minutes, 40 seconds?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's at the same position at what is presently to be seen on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, it says 20.43. That's when the mortar at Bogosica Park appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was getting that on to the record, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I would like to thank my colleague, Ms. Somers, for giving me this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Somers, if you would be able to resume your cross-examination. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pleasure, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, you indicated that Ivanica was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was I correct in my understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Ivanica, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that was -- what is the importance of -- well, sorry, let me rephrase it so I don't confuse you. Who among your company commanders was at Ivanica? When I say "your company commanders," I mean the company commanders of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I was at Ivanica specifically speaking with my unit. In the broader area of Ivanica, of the settlement of Ivanica, were Captain Stojanovic, Captain Jeremic, Lieutenant Lemal --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which Captain -- do you know Captain Jeremic's first name, his first name?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Zlatan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From what period of time were you at Ivanica? From when to when?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not going to be very precise in terms of these dates. But it's from the end of September, the 25th or the 26th of September, until the end of October. The 27th or 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the -- as of 6 of December, whose command post, if anyone's, were at Ivanica? Let's put it 5th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: We cannot say command post in a way. If we are talking about a company, it's not a command post, it's an observation post. That's its official name. At Ivanica, there was Captain Jeremic and the logistics part of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is Brgat?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain this to you. Maybe the best way would be to use a map. Leaving from Ivanica --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me start this way. In which republic was Brgat found or is it found? Is it in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is it in Montenegro? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Brgat is in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how far is Brgat from Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Depending from what point we measure the distance, and it is approximately between 1 and a half and 2 kilometres, straight line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And on the 5th of December 1991, whose command was located at Brgat?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I told you that it was Captain Jeremic's and the logistics part of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At Brgat?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Oh, you're talking about Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right, I'm talking about Brgat.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The battalion's command post was at Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then that's the battalion that was commanded by Captain Vladimir Kovacevic. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That was specifically the 3rd Battalion's command post, and we were part of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated today during your examination-in-chief on page 14, roughly, lines 6 and 7 -- sorry, 6 through 9, you indicated that you were informed that you should go and report at the command or to the command. You would be having a briefing at the command of the commander of the mortar company, Captain Jeremic at Ivanica, to be very precise. Do you remember saying that today?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you met with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in a very official army building in Belgrade, September 2nd, 2003. Do you remember the meeting at which you gave a statement that was recorded? Do you remember that? The question was asked you about where the meeting on the 5th was held, and in the English, it's a bit difficult. But you were asked: "Now, were these orders given at the battalion headquarters?" You said: "We were in a different building. We were not in the building where the battalion headquarters were actually located." "And so this was not -- basically the battalion commander had assembled his company commanders in a specific location just for this briefing away from the headquarters?" Your answer was: "Yes, we met in a different building and the building belonged to one of the company commanders."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "We met in a different building, and that building belonged to one of the company commanders." Question: "Was that within the area?" Answer: "I believe it was Brgat. The Brgat region." Now, was it Brgat or was it Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: That was at Ivanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you told the Office of the Prosecutor it was in the Brgat region.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. That is what I said. After I read the transcript, I noticed this mistake because at the time when we discussed this, how it came about, it could be that Ivanica and Brgat were interchanged and that a mistake was made. Later, during the conversation, it becomes evident that it was at the command of the mortar company headquarters or command, that is Captain Zlatan Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... suggesting that the term "battalion headquarters" was inappropriate; that it was always company headquarters. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I am not ascertaining that. In this specific situation, we had debriefing session at the company commander's command. That is, Captain Zlatan Jeremic was the commander of the mortar company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before that question that I just asked you was asked, another question was asked of you: "Was there a set of orders written for this attack? Or the orders were given verbally at the battalion headquarters?" Your answer -- and the question was "battalion headquarters": "Verbal orders." Now that's two times battalion headquarters was mentioned. Did you not think it appropriate to correct at the time, after all twice it was mentioned? What suddenly made you decide to say Ivanica instead of Brgat today in court?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Because that is what is correct. And secondly, you'll remember during that conversation the translation was incorrect most of the time when it referred to the battalion headquarters, and that is what it says in my transcript as well. Once I also had to intervene about the translation and deny that that was not what I said, that my words were incorrectly translated. And then the translator, Ms. Biljana, corrected herself that it was not a document as she referred to, but that it was a term as it was. Therefore, these mistakes could happen in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you noticed this, did you ask Defence counsel who were working with you before you came to court today to make the correction?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask any corrections to be made because I didn't think it was of any significance because we all understood what it was referred to as headquarters of the battalion, that in fact it was the command battalion -- battalion command during the conversation that we had in Belgrade. And I never insisted that this should be literally translated as command instead of headquarters or main staff or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If someone addressed you as Corporal Nesic, would you correct it to say, "no, that's Colonel Nesic." Would you insist on a correction of terms?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It depends on the situation that I'm in. If somebody who is not related to the military would address me in that way, I would only laugh. However, if I were in a direct relationship with a superior officer, then probably I would react, not in a heated fashion. I would probably also laugh again and draw their attention to my correct rank. In my encounters with various people, and I know many people, among them are my cadets, I will still be addressed by them as second lieutenant because most of them had known me at that time, and they would always refer to me in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you use the term "early evening," what time of day are you referring to? What does that mean to you, the term "early evening" which you used today in evidence? Please give us a time of day.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: "Early evening" means, for instance, now, today in The Hague would be -- even 10.30 in the evening, and that is at the time when dark fell. And that is my benchmark that I use, and that is the time when it becomes dark. So early evening is immediately after dark falls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: December 1991 or December pretty much any year in the Dubrovnik area, when does it become dark? We're talking wintertime. When does it become dark?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, basically at around 6.00 p.m. or 6.30, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you make any kind of a note anywhere about the times you were called and the locations to which you were called for any types of meetings or briefings? Do you keep any type of record so that if you were asked to explain, you're able to document it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I made notes in my notebook that I used at the time where I entered the dates, the reports, the tasks assigned to me, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Nesic, I put to you that in the winter in Dubrovnik that darkness begins -- the sun begins to go down between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon, the sun begins to go down, and it becomes toward dark. That is correct? You were there, weren't you? You know that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Whether it's at 3.00 or 4.00, I don't think it is that early. But definitely after 4.00 in the afternoon because it's at the seaside, and it becomes dark rather later than in the mountainous areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So when you refer to "early evening," you're talking about a time frame around 4.00, as it becomes dark?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about the period after 4.00 if we want to be very specific about the time. I'm talking about early evening when it's already become dark, but it was not in some late evening hours, for instance, after 10.00 p.m. or 2100 hours. But rather in the early evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated you received a call from a soldier about a meeting or a briefing. Please tell us who was the soldier, from what unit, and exactly, and I mean exactly what he told you.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say from a soldier. I said from the communications operator. He's the one in charge of communications equipment. And 13 years later, it is really impossible for me to repeat verbatim what he told me. But basically, he said that I was to come to Ivanica for debriefing and that the commander would be there after his debriefing in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to know exactly what time, and your exact words were, "a soldier, a communications soldier." I want to know exactly what time that communications soldier told you to report to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I really cannot say the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Give us an approximation.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately it was at about one hour or half an hour before I was supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So give an approximate time, please. You're a commander. You are a responsible person. Tell us the time.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I really cannot remember what time it was on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What time were you supposed to report to Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: We had regular debriefing sessions normally between 1900 or 2000 hours. Sometimes earlier, from 6.00 p.m. until 7.00 p.m. But mainly in that period, depending on how much time the battalion commander spent at his debriefing session at the forward command post in Kupari and after he returned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So if we put your estimate of one and a half hours before, that would make it around 4.30 that you got your call?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I made a note of half an hour, not one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're absolutely right. I thought it was "an hour and a half."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we take it the one-hour mark, does that make it around 5.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. Within that time frame, because at 1700 hours the debriefing would begin at the forward command post at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, are you able to indicate what time it was when you actually got there?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I didn't pay attention. I know that I make it in time and that I was there before the battalion command arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you wear a watch, Colonel, at the time? Was it your habit to wear a watch or timepiece of some kind?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Of course. I always wear a watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you yourself ever been to a briefing at the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, on the 8th, I went to the forward command post at Kupari, and that's when I wrote my report concerning the operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Right. Now, the daily or regular briefings at Kupari, was that your habit? Were you invited to attend those? Were you at such a level that you would attend the briefings at Kupari on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Madam, that was not the usual thing, nor did we go. I was the company commander, and company commanders don't attend briefings or meetings like that. The lowest level is battalion commander among the people who are there, or perhaps the officer who stands in for him if he happens to be absent from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how you know what time briefings at Kupari would go, and particularly on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew. Every briefing that we held, even if it was just a normal conversation, if during the day the commander, for example, said, "I have to be at Kupari for the briefing by 5.00."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what, if any, unusual events from the standpoint of negotiations or the overall fate of Dubrovnik was the subject of various meetings on the 5th of December? What do you know about what was happening in your area, by your area, I mean the area of the 2nd Operational Group, on the 5th of December? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: You're really asking me questions that I can't answer. Do you know at all what the area was of the 2nd Operational Group? I was a company commander, and my area was about 600 or 700 metres. How would I have been in a position to know what was happening in the area of the 2nd Operational Group which was covering a vast area?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of which your company was part, Colonel. Now, what was -- I'm sorry. Of which your company was a part, Colonel. Now, what events of importance did you know about happening on the 5th of December? Do you communicate with any of your colleagues? Do you read any of the briefing reports? What was happening the 5th of December, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, nothing special was happening in my unit. I did meet other company commanders at the briefing, and we exchanged the usual kind of information. It was just the usual kind of conversation that we would have, how each of us were feeling, whether there were any particular problems, that sort of thing. There was nothing special for me to put forward about anything happening, anything along these lines in terms of operations being carried out, if that's what you had in mind, or anything special, anything peculiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, the hostilities, the fighting in the Dubrovnik area was winding down and was to come to an end, wasn't it? And those negotiations were taking place on the 5th of December. You were a company commander. And although you may not have been the highest ranking officer, you knew that there were negotiations pending, didn't you? You heard about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't heard anything about any negotiations being afoot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, there was a cease-fire in effect from November, was there not, as of the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long did the briefing last that you attended at Ivanica or that you say was at Ivanica?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It took place at Ivanica, and it lasted about one and a half hours. I can't really can't say specifically, but thereabouts, one and a half hours. There were the usual things that were being said, but there were also other things that were being said that were not related to the regular situation in the units, but also there were other elements that were being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did Zoran Lemal arrive at the briefing? You know him, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was there in time. Before the battalion commander arrived. Now, I can't give you the exact time. Really, I can't. But he was there in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did the battalion commander arrive? Give a time frame, please. When did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Madam, if I give you a rough estimate, then it cannot be accurate. I'm telling you again, I really can't remember what time it was exactly. And anything I say may be an error, which is something that I wish to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, now, regular briefings were held, were they not, involving the battalion commander? He would appear at the regular briefings for your company, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: The briefing in my company, no, the battalion commander didn't come to those briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The person who did the most talking at this briefing was who?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Of course, the battalion commander, each of the company commanders talked about the situation in their own respective units. And then the battalion commander, having heard what the situation was across the units, would ask certain questions if anything was still not clear, and then finally he would issue tasks for further activities, the general kind of activity that applied to all the units. And then specific tasks for specific units or maybe talked to individual commanders and issue more precise instructions for certain tasks or whatever else there was to be done. This was a general situation, and this is the way it was usually done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, now, you seem to be switched on or in the loop on when Captain Kovacevic reported to briefings at Kupari. Would you be good enough to tell us when he reported to briefings at Kupari in the month of October. Would it be around the same time as you have it now? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No. Throughout October, Captain Kovacevic never went to Kupari for briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what about November?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did go for briefings in November at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what times did he go for briefings in early November at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Usually it would be at about 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where was he going from that you would be aware of what time he would be going to Kupari? What was he departing from?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: If you want me to talk about specific dates, I didn't exactly follow him. I wasn't shadowing him, which position he was leaving, whether he was leaving from the command, from my company or a different company. This is something that I can't answer. What I'm telling you is when he -- whenever he was back from Kupari, he would tell us that he had been to Kupari for a briefing or he would come and tell us, "I have to be at Kupari today by 5.00."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, I want you to tell me, Colonel, when in early November he reported to Kupari for briefings. I want you to give me a time in early November. You said October no, but November yes. Tell me when in early November.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Madam, as for the exact time when he left for Kupari, this is something that I can't tell you. Briefings were organised in such a way that they would begin at 5.00 p.m. in Kupari so that the unit commanders could go back to their units once the briefing was over. They could inform their own officers, issue tasks, and explain tasks to company commanders, and still have enough time to convey these tasks to their companies during the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. That's helpful. Now, that would be the same for the briefings he would attend in early November, the first early days of November. Is that correct? It would apply to those days as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, please, that you be shown P101. P101.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, this document which is in evidence is dated 20th of November 1991. And it indicates that from that date, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade would be directly subordinated to the 9th VPS, and that has its headquarters at Kupari, does it not, its forward command post? Right? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Will you please just give me a moment to find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me a hand. I'm not sure what line that's on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you look at the first paragraph, it says: "The 472nd Motorised Brigade without the 3rd Motorised Battalion," and then it goes on to describe. It talks about "the brigade shall leave... " Let me help you out. Then right after it, says: "Pursuant to a decision of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group," and it gives an order number of 19 November "shall leave the complement of the 9th VPS and work on orders from the 2nd OG" and it shows parentheses, "2nd Corps." Do you see that? Did you find it on the document? It's basically right under 1.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the forward command post of the 9th VPS is at Kupari, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So only from, let's say, 20th of November would the commander of that battalion which has just been put under the immediate subordination of the 9th VPS report to Kupari. Wouldn't that be logical? Wouldn't that be according to military order?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: No, in terms of military order, that wouldn't necessarily make sense. First you have the -- up in the heading --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, let me put to you that up until the 20th of November, the battalion commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade was reporting to the brigade headquarters, which are not at Kupari, so I have no idea in early November or up to the 20th when he would report to Kupari because he wasn't reporting to Kupari. And that is borne out by this document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Madam, if you were standing right next to him and you watched him going wherever it was that he was going, well, then, all right. I wasn't exactly standing next to him, but I know what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So if, in fact, the 3rd Battalion was still reporting to the brigade up until the 20th of November, your comment about reporting to Kupari in the early part of November is simply wrong, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: Madam, that's not right what you're saying. Once I had reached Zarkovica, I never saw another officer from the battalion command [as interpreted]. I only saw officers from the command of the 9th VPS. And this went on until the end of May 1992, which is when I returned to Ivanica which was where we had withdrawn with our unit. And then again, officers from the command of the Trebinje Brigade started to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 75, line 20, it says: "Battalion command," whereas the witness actually said "brigade command." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Simply put, Colonel, you have no idea if or where or what he was doing in the early days of November, and you don't know -- you know that he couldn't have reported to Kupari. He wasn't directly subordinated. I mean, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: It's not right, Madam. Our battalion from the time it was introduced into combat, from that very moment, it was subordinated to the 9th VPS in order to carry out tasks in the areas of Bosanka and Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a briefing at the brigade headquarters of the 472nd? Do you know where the brigade headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA NESIC
utterances.text: I know that the brigade command was at Trebinje. Of course, I didn't attend the briefings. It was for the same kind of rank as the forward command post of the 9th VPS. I just didn't attend. Therefore, I can't say anything about those. A while ago when I said by rote [Realtime transcript read in error "by road"], I said Bosanka and Brgat. When I meant is just Bosanka, without Brgat because Brgat had already been taken by late October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it should read "by rote," not "by road."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have more cross-examination tomorrow. I don't know what point the Chamber wishes to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we're a minute or two early. But is that really a logical point, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think it would be good, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll adjourn then for the evening, and we'll resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning, and I believe we will be in Courtroom Number I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of July, 2004, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
